question: Can all beings attain buddhahood, or are there beings (icchantikas, those without lineage) who never will?

sides.position: All sentient beings have buddha-nature, including the icchantika; there is no fixed icchantika; all will attain buddhahood.
arguments: All beings are tathāgatagarbhas because the dharmakāya pervades them, suchness is undivided and the lineage is present (RGV 1.27-28).
'All beings have buddha-nature — even the icchantikas; because they will surely attain unsurpassed awakening in the future it is said all have it' (Mahāparinirvāṇa juan 27).
One who understands the four alternatives should not insist that the icchantika definitely lacks it (juan 36).
The Lotus: there is only one vehicle and all who hear become buddhas.

sides.position: Beings have distinct lineages (gotra); some belong to the śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha lineage and some have no lineage (agotra) and do not attain buddhahood; the teaching of universal buddha-nature was given with a hidden intention.
arguments: The Laṅkāvatāra lists five lineages, the fifth being 'no lineage'.

The icchantika who has abandoned the roots of merit by rejecting the bodhisattva collection does not enter nirvāṇa (Laṅkāvatāra p. 28) — though it adds that the Tathāgata's power may revive his roots.
The Saṃdhinirmocana (ch. 7) says the śrāvaka of fixed lineage cannot be led to awakening even by all buddhas; the one vehicle was taught with an intention (from memory, chapter-level).

sides.position: Faxian's six-fascicle Nirvāṇa Sūtra (418) and its first Chinese readers: icchantikas are excluded from buddha-nature.
arguments: The early part of the Mahāparinirvāṇa says icchantikas, having cut off the roots of good, lack buddha-nature (in the sense of wholesome qualities) (T374 juan 26 retains this).

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: each side uses the tradition's own P5/P6 hermeneutic to make the other's teaching provisional, so the principle cannot decide between them.
candidate_readings: P5 (Yogācāra reading): 'all have buddha-nature' is neyārtha, spoken to encourage beings of indeterminate lineage.
P5/P6 (Tathāgatagarbha and Tiantai reading): the five-lineage teaching is a skillful means; the one vehicle and universal buddha-nature are nītārtha.
P4 (Mahāparinirvāṇa juan 36 and Laṅkāvatāra p. 28 themselves): 'icchantika' names a present condition, not an eternal nature — the Tathāgata's power can revive the roots of good.
P1 (Faxiang's own distinction, reported from memory): buddha-nature as principle (lixing) all beings have; buddha-nature as practice (xingxing) some lack.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Tiantai/Tendai and Huayan reject any being permanently without buddhahood; the Faxiang/Hossō tradition rejects universal attainment as the definitive teaching.

historical_debates.name: Daosheng on the icchantika
historical_debates.accounts: Daosheng taught, against the six-fascicle Nirvāṇa Sūtra, that icchantikas too can become buddhas and was expelled from the capital's saṅgha; when Dharmakṣema's 40-fascicle version arrived it contained that teaching.

historical_debates.name: The 'three-one' controversy (Saichō and Tokuitsu)
historical_debates.accounts: Saichō (Tendai) defended the one vehicle and universal buddha-nature; Tokuitsu (Hossō) defended the three vehicles and the five lineages.
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Each school claimed victory; Tendai's position became dominant in Japan.

question: Is the one vehicle the final truth and the three vehicles a skillful means — or are the three vehicles real and the 'one vehicle' spoken with an intention?

sides.position: One vehicle only: the three vehicles are the Buddha's skillful means to lead beings into the one buddha-vehicle (Lotus; Śrīmālā); the arhat's nirvāṇa is a conjured city.
arguments: There is no second or third vehicle anywhere in the ten directions (Lotus 2).
The father gives all his children the one great cart (Lotus 3).
The two vehicles enter the great vehicle; the arhat still has the ground of ignorance (Śrīmālā 5).

sides.position: The three vehicles correspond to real differences of lineage; the 'one vehicle' was taught with an intention (the sameness of the dharma-realm, of no-self and of liberation), to attract the indeterminate.
arguments: The Laṅkāvatāra's five lineages.
The Saṃdhinirmocana ch. 7: the one vehicle is taught with an intention; the fixed-lineage śrāvaka cannot reach awakening (chapter-level, from memory).

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: both sides apply upāya/neyārtha, in opposite directions.
candidate_readings: Lotus/Tiantai: the three are upāya (P6), the one is nītārtha.
Yogācāra/Faxiang: the one is abhiprāya-speech (P5), the three are nītārtha.
Stage reading (P4): three vehicles for beings at different stages, one vehicle as the eventual end for all.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Tiantai insists the Lotus's one vehicle is the final 'perfect' teaching; Faxiang insists on fixed lineages.

historical_debates.name: Three carts or four carts
historical_debates.accounts: Readers of the burning-house parable divided on whether the great ox-cart given at the end is the bodhisattva's ox-cart of the three (the 'three-cart' reading of Faxiang and Sanlun exegetes) or a fourth, great white-ox cart (the 'four-cart' reading of Tiantai and Huayan).

question: Which turning of the dharma-wheel is of definitive meaning (nītārtha): the teaching of emptiness (second) or the 'well-distinguished' teaching of the three natures and of buddha-nature (third)?

sides.position: The sūtras teaching emptiness, the signless, no self and no being are definitive; those teaching self, a being, or a truly existent base are provisional (Akṣayamati); the tathāgatagarbha is emptiness taught with an intention (Laṅkāvatāra).
arguments: The Akṣayamatinirdeśa's criterion of nītārtha.
The Laṅkāvatāra's own gloss of the tathāgatagarbha as emptiness taught to remove fear of no-self.
Candrakīrti (Madhyamakāvatāra 6.94-95, U40) reads the Laṅkāvatāra so.

sides.position: The first two turnings are surpassable and provisional; the third, which distinguishes the three natures and three naturelessnesses, is unsurpassed and definitive (Saṃdhinirmocana ch. 7).
arguments: The Saṃdhinirmocana's own statement about the three turnings.

sides.position: The third turning's tathāgatagarbha sūtras and the Ratnagotravibhāga are definitive: the ultimate (dharmakāya, buddha-nature) is empty of what is other than it — the adventitious stains — and not empty of its own qualities (shentong).
arguments: Śrīmālā ch. 9 and RGV 1.154-155: empty of stains, not empty of qualities.
Dolpopa's Mountain Doctrine (U48).

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: P5 is the Buddhist traditions' own hermeneutic and all sides accept it, but it names the distinction without settling its application.
candidate_readings: Rimé reading (Jamgön Kongtrul, U48): the second turning is definitive about the emptiness of the relative, the third about the ultimate — both definitive in their own sphere.
Stage reading (P4): the turnings addressed disciples of different capacities (Saṃdhinirmocana itself).
Madhyamaka reading: third-turning statements are provisional (P5) but purposeful (RGV 1.156-157, P6).
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Gelug rejects the shentong reading; Jonang rejects the reading of the third turning as provisional.

question: Is buddha-nature a true self (permanent, blissful, pure, not empty of qualities) or another name for emptiness?

sides.position: Buddha-nature is the true self: 'self means the tathāgatagarbha'; the dharmakāya has the perfection of self; the garbha is not empty of the inseparable buddha-qualities.
arguments: 'No-self is saṃsāra, self is the Tathāgata' (Mahāparinirvāṇa juan 2).
'Self means the tathāgatagarbha' (juan 7).
Śrīmālā 9 and 12; RGV 1.35.
Aṅgulimālīya.

sides.position: The tathāgatagarbha is not the self of the tīrthikas: the buddhas teach it meaning emptiness, the reality-limit, nirvāṇa, the unborn, so that the foolish may not fear no-self; its purpose is to remove five faults.
arguments: Laṅkāvatāra p. 33.
RGV 1.156-157: taught to remove discouragement, contempt, etc.

sides.position: (East Asian reading from the same sūtra) Buddha-nature is the emptiness of the highest meaning, which sees both empty and non-empty — the middle way.
arguments: Mahāparinirvāṇa juan 27.

reconciliation.explanation: The texts themselves distinguish levels — the Mahāparinirvāṇa separates worldly and supramundane 'self', and the Laṅkāvatāra and RGV state the teaching's purpose — so 'self' and 'no-self' refer to different objects (the dharmakāya's qualities vs the imagined self of the aggregates).
reconciliation.detail: Under P1 the 'self' of the garbha is the ultimate-level perfection of the dharmakāya and 'no-self' denies the self imagined in the aggregates; under P6 the Laṅkāvatāra says the garbha-teaching is skillful means. What remains open is whether the garbha's 'self' is itself definitive (P5) — see dsp:which-turning-is-definitive.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: The Jonang and many East Asian readers hold the self-language definitive, not skillful means; Gelug holds buddha-nature to be the mind's emptiness and rejects any non-empty absolute; Theravāda rejects any self at all (dsp:is-there-a-self).

question: Are the Mahāyāna sūtras the word of the Buddha?

sides.position: Yes: they were taught by the Buddha to bodhisattva assemblies (and some kept by nāgas until beings could receive them); rejecting them is grave karma.
arguments: Rejecting the perfection of wisdom leads to the hells (Aṣṭa 7).
One who rejects the bodhisattva collection as not conducive to liberation becomes an icchantika (Laṅkāvatāra p. 28).
Arguments of the Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra ch. 1 (U41).

sides.position: No: the Buddha's word is what was recited at the councils; the 'Vetulla' (Vaitulya) teachings are not the Buddha's word.
arguments: The Kathāvatthu refutes Vetullaka views (e.g. that the Buddha did not himself teach the dharma) (U37).
The Sri Lankan chronicles report kings suppressing the Vetullavāda at the Abhayagiri (from memory).

reconciliation.explanation: Not yet reconciled: an authenticity question that none of the eight principles decides.
candidate_readings: P4: sūtras addressed to disciples of higher capacity, not recited in the śrāvaka councils (the Mahāyāna's own account).
P5: the Mahāyāna sūtras as the definitive intent of what the earlier sūtras taught provisionally (Mahāyāna reading) — rejected by Theravāda.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Theravāda rejects the Mahāyāna sūtras as buddhavacana; the Mahāyāna rejects the council criterion as the only test.

historical_debates.name: Suppression of the Vetullavāda in Anurādhapura
historical_debates.accounts: The Mahāvaṃsa reports that kings (Vohārika Tissa; later Goṭhābhaya) suppressed the Vetullavāda associated with the Abhayagiri monastery.
historical_debates.outcome_by_tradition: Theravāda (Mahāvihāra) orthodoxy restored, per the chronicle; details from memory, low confidence.

question: Is the Tathāgata permanent (his parinirvāṇa a display), or is parinirvāṇa the final end, the Tathāgata after death being undeclared?

sides.position: The Tathāgata's lifespan is immeasurable; he awakened aeons ago and shows parinirvāṇa as skillful means; his body is the dharmakāya, the vajra body, permanent.
arguments: Lotus 16; Golden Light ch. 2; Vimalakīrti 3.44; Mahāparinirvāṇa juan 3.

sides.position: At parinibbāna the Tathāgata is released from reckoning by the aggregates; whether he exists after death is not declared; like a fire gone out he cannot be said to have gone anywhere.
arguments: The fire simile of the Aggivacchagotta Sutta (MN 72).
The undeclared questions.

reconciliation.explanation: Both deny that the Tathāgata can be reckoned by the aggregates; the Mahāyāna calls the undescribable dharmakāya 'permanent' at the ultimate level and the parinirvāṇa an upāya.
reconciliation.detail: The Pali 'deep, immeasurable, hard to fathom' Tathāgata (MN 72) and the Vajracchedikā's Tathāgata who 'neither comes nor goes' meet under P1; the Lotus's eternal display is P6.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Theravāda rejects the positive assertion of a permanent Tathāgata as a view (sassatavāda) and rejects the parinibbāna as a mere display.

sides.position: No: the bodhisattva, seeing all beings as his only child and as former relatives, must not eat meat; the earlier permission of 'three-fold pure' meat was given step by step and is now withdrawn.
arguments: Laṅkāvatāra ch. 8.
Mahāparinirvāṇa juan 4: 'eating meat cuts off the seed of great compassion'.
Brahmajāla minor precept on meat.

sides.position: Meat that is pure in three respects (not seen, heard or suspected to have been killed for the monk) may be accepted; the Buddha refused Devadatta's demand to make abstention from meat compulsory.
arguments: Jīvaka Sutta (MN 55).
Devadatta's five points (Vinaya, Cullavagga 7).

reconciliation.explanation: The Mahāparinirvāṇa itself presents the three-fold-pure rule as a provisional, stage-by-stage permission later withdrawn for bodhisattvas.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Theravāda holds the three-fold-pure rule to be the Buddha's final rule and the Laṅkāvatāra's chapter (absent from its earliest Chinese version) not the Buddha's word; Tibetan traditions have varied in practice.

question: Can a woman, in a woman's body, attain buddhahood?

sides.position: Womanhood is empty like all dharmas: dharmas are neither male nor female (the goddess in Vimalakīrti); Queen Śrīmālā teaches the one vehicle and is predicted to buddhahood; the goddess of the Ganges is predicted; the nāga princess attains buddhahood in an instant.
arguments: Vimalakīrti 6.14-16.
Śrīmālā ch. 1.
Aṣṭasāhasrikā ch. 19.
Lotus ch. 12.

sides.position: A woman's body cannot be a buddha: Śāriputra objects so in the Lotus, and the nāga princess becomes male before appearing as a buddha; Amitābha's and Bhaiṣajyaguru's vows promise women release from the woman's state; the Pali Bahudhātuka Sutta (MN 115) says a woman cannot be a fully awakened buddha.
arguments: Lotus 12 (Śāriputra's objection; the transformation).
Bhaiṣajyaguru's vows.

reconciliation.explanation: The Vimalakīrti itself places the question on two levels: ultimately dharmas are neither male nor female; conventionally bodies and their karmic conditions are spoken of.
reconciliation.detail: Under P1 the goddess's teaching (ultimate) and the sex-change narratives and vows (conventional) do not exclude each other; whether the conventional condition binds final buddhahood is not settled by P1.
reconciliation.tradition_objections: Traditions that hold the thirty-two marks (including the male mark) to be required of a buddha keep the conventional restriction as binding.
